chunk_findings.detail: The docstring promises "digests … whose cited lines **the commits since the reviewed head** rewrote", and the function even computes the current head (`tip`) to verify `head` is still an ancestor — but `tip` is then discarded and the diff handed to `SS.superseded_digests` is taken between the *old* reviewed head and the worktree's configured base ref, i.e. the already-reviewed range (`base_ref..head`, the very diff the findings were written against), not the fix commits (`head..tip`). Concrete case: branch at head `H` was round-1 reviewed, findings cite lines that exist only in `H`; a child commit `T` then fixes them. `_superseded` checks `H` is an ancestor of `T`, then calls `_delta_diff(..., H, base_ref)` instead of `_delta_diff(..., T, H)` (or `(..., H, T)` depending on argument order — neither endpoint is `tip`), so `superseded_digests` is fed the old reviewed diff. Either it considers the cited lines "present/rewritten" because they appear in that diff, in which case `new` is the whole prior finding set, `_is_fix_round` returns true, and still-valid findings are silently dropped from `has_unaddressed_findings`/carried as superseded; or (if it requires a removed-then-replaced line) it returns nothing, `a["supers_new"]` is empty, `_is_fix_round` can never be true, and the reported bug (stale findings re-reported because the reviewer is shown only unrelated chunks) is not fixed at all. In both readings the fix commits `head..tip` never enter the computation, which is the only range that can tell whether a cited line was rewritten since the review.

chunk_findings.detail: The branch decides a prior finding is "SUPERSEDED" purely because its digest is in `supers`, i.e. because the lines it cites were *rewritten since the reviewed commit* — as the appended text itself states — and then instructs the reviewer "do NOT report it again". A line being rewritten is not evidence that the reported defect was resolved: a fix commit can touch the cited line (reorder it, add a comment/guard, rename a local, reformat a multi-line expression) while the original defect still holds. Input demonstrating it: round-1 finding `[HIGH] ddflow/api/exec.py:412 execute(): serially serialises str(srv.called_from)`; the fix commit rewrites line 412 by hoisting `str(srv.called_from)` into a variable but still serialising it. `supers` now contains that finding's digest, so the prompt says "SUPERSEDED: the lines it cites were rewritten ... do NOT report it again", the reviewer drops a finding that is still true, and the defect ships. The instruction is also self-contradictory ("do NOT report it again -- judge the new code only"), so the outcome depends on which half the model follows. If the goal is "drop findings whose cited lines no longer exist", the drop must be keyed on the cited code being gone/replaced *and* the finding re-checked against the current code, not on a digest of "this line changed".

chunk_findings.detail: The `--- /dev/null` guard only suppresses the *header* branch; it does not stop the line from falling through to the removed-line branch below it. When a diff contains a real file whose hunks have been walked (so `path` is set and `pos > 0`) followed by a newly-added file, the parser hits the new file's `--- /dev/null` line: `_FILE.match` succeeds but the `if` is false, `_HUNK` fails, and then `elif pos and path and line.startswith("-")` is true (the line starts with `-`, `path`/`pos` still belong to the *previous* file), so it appends `(pos, pos)` to the previous file and increments `pos`. Given, e.g., a diff whose last hunk of `old.py` ends with `pos == 13` followed by `--- /dev/null` / `+++ b/new.py`, `changed_old_lines` returns `old.py -> [(..., (13, 13))]` even though line 13 of `old.py` was never touched. Any finding whose `location` is `old.py:13` then gets `is_superseded(...) == True`, its digest lands in `superseded_digests(...)`, and a legitimate round‑1 finding is silently dropped as "already rewritten" instead of being re‑checked (exactly the false-negative direction the module is supposed to avoid). The same fall-through is also reachable when a *removed content line* happens to start with `-- ` (diff line `--- ...`), where the real deletion is not counted at all because the line is misread as a file header. The header branch needs to `continue`/reset `pos` unconditionally (or the removed-line branch needs to exclude `--- `/`-`-prefixed header lines).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review_supersede.py:24 (`changed_old_lines`)

chunk_findings.detail: This asserts, and thereby locks in, that a finding cited without a line number is treated as *superseded* whenever any line of that file is rewritten by the later commit — and `test_a_finding_on_rewritten_lines_is_superseded_not_reraised` then pins the consequence (`SUPERSEDED` in the prompt, `triage: untriaged` suppressed, `fix_round is True`). Take the repo's own example from the bug report: a round‑1 finding recorded as `shell.py` (or any symbol-only citation, e.g. "footer() still returns the restart note without consulting reexec"), and a later commit that rewrites an unrelated line in `shell.py`. `changed_old_lines` returns a non-empty range list for `shell.py`, so `is_superseded("shell.py", ch)` is `True`, the finding is handed to the reviewer labelled `SUPERSEDED` instead of being judged against the current code of the file it names, the untriaged re-raise is suppressed, and the round is scored as a free fix round. The stated expectation for Be1818cd552 is to judge prior findings against the current code of the named files, or drop only those "whose cited lines no longer exist" — for a file-only citation the file (and all its lines) still exists, so neither alternative applies. This is the over-broad half of the supersede rule, encoded in the test that is supposed to protect against stale/false findings; with file-scoped citations present it turns "stale finding re-raised" into "live finding written off as superseded and the budget round consumed for free".

chunk_findings.detail:
`_is_fix_round` classifies a round as a free "pure fix round" only when every finding of the last round is either in `a["supers"]` (its cited lines were rewritten) or has triage verdict **`"confirmed"`**. It ignores findings whose triage verdict is `"refuted"`, even though the rest of this module treats `refuted` and `confirmed` as equivalent "settled, no further action" states (`_SETTLED = ("refuted", "confirmed")`, and the very next function excludes both from the pending count at line ~496). A refuted finding needs no fix and its lines normally are not rewritten, so it is neither in `a["supers"]` nor `== "confirmed"`.

Concrete failure: round 1 yields f1 and f2; triage refutes f1 and confirms f2; the author commits a fix for f2, rewriting its lines. On re-review with `[review].fix_round_free`, `_superseded` returns `new = {f2}` so `a["supers_new"]` is non-empty and the loop over `found` reaches f1: `f1 not in a["supers"]` and its verdict is `"refuted"`, not `"confirmed"` → `all(...)` is False → `_is_fix_round` returns False. The round is therefore treated as an ordinary delta round that consumes the round budget (the `and not a["fix"]` guard is bypassed from the wrong side), which is exactly the extra re-review/triage cost the change is supposed to remove, for the very common case where round 1 contained any finding the triager rejected. The docstring's own rule ("commits since the reviewed head addressed EVERY finding") already holds here, since a refuted finding is addressed; the code should accept `verdict in _SETTLED` (or `not in ("", None)`) rather than `== "confirmed"`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new branch does not drop a stale finding — it keeps the finding’s full header/detail text in the prompt and then appends an absolute instruction: “do NOT report this finding again”. Combined with the definition given in the message itself (“the lines it cites were rewritten since the reviewed commit”), the suppression condition is broader than the failure the change is supposed to catch (the intent says drop only findings “whose cited lines no longer exist”). Concretely: suppose round‑1 reported finding B against `footer()` citing lines 1740–1744, and the later “fix” commit for an *unrelated* finding A edits one of those same lines (adds a parameter, inserts a guard, reformats the block — very common when A and B live in the same function). `supers` then contains B’s digest, so this loop emits only the SUPERSEDED note instead of B’s triage and tells the reviewer never to re-report it, even though B’s defect (e.g. `footer()` still not consulting `freeexec`) is untouched by A’s commit. The result is a silent false negative — a still-broken HEAD is passed by the gate — which is a worse outcome than the 12 hand-triage calls the bug report was about. The correct predicate is “the cited lines no longer exist / the defect can no longer be located”, not “some line in the cited span changed”; if the decision is to annotate rather than drop, the annotation must not be an unconditional “never report this”, since the code that generated it cannot distinguish an edit that fixed the finding from one that merely landed on the same lines.

chunk_findings.detail: `_LOC` requires the path to contain a dot followed by word characters (`([\w./+@-]+\.\w+)`), so any file name without an extension (or a leading-dot name) is never recognised as `path:line`; `is_superseded` then takes the `if not m: return False` branch and reports the finding as *not* superseded, exactly the stale-finding behaviour this change is supposed to eliminate. Concrete: with `changed = {"Makefile": [(10, 10)]}` (the HEAD commit rewrote old line 10 of `Makefile`) and a prior finding whose location is `"Makefile:10"`, `_LOC.search("Makefile:10")` finds no match and `is_superseded` returns `False`, so the round-2 reviewer is again asked to re-check a line that no longer exists and can answer "does not touch X, so the finding stands". The same holds for `"Dockerfile:3"`, `".gitignore:7"`, etc. The docstring at lines 44-47 promises this is only true for a *bare path or a symbol* ("that finding is re-checked"); `Makefile:10` does name a line, so returning `False` contradicts the function's contract and leaves the reported bug (Be1818cd552) unfixed for these files.

chunk_findings.detail:
The file-header test (`line.startswith("--- ") and nxt.startswith("+++ ")`) is applied to every line of the diff, including lines inside a hunk, and matches a removed line whose content begins with `-- ` followed by an added line whose content begins with `++ `. Given a diff such as

```
--- a/patch.py
+++ b/patch.py
@@ -1,5 +1,5 @@
 a
--- old
+++ new
 b
-c
+d
```

the removed line `-- old` is rendered as `--- old` and the added line `++ new` as `+++ new`, so the branch fires: `path` is reset to `"old"` and `pos` to `0`. From then on `elif pos and path ...` is false, so the real removal of line 5 (`-c`) is never recorded and `changed["patch.py"]` stays empty; a fixed finding located at `patch.py:5` is therefore not superseded and is carried forward. Any diff of a file that contains `-- ` / `++ ` lines (patch fixtures, diffs-of-diffs) triggers this.

chunk_findings.detail:
Making the path group extension-optional — `([\w./+@-]+)` instead of `([\w./+@-]+\.\w+)` — turns `_LOC` into a pattern that matches an arbitrary leading word. `_LOC` is unanchored and is applied with `search` over the finding's citation text (that is precisely why the old pattern required `\.\w+`: so a bare prose word would fail and `search` would skip ahead to the real `path:line`). With the new pattern, `search` now returns the *leftmost* match, i.e. the first word, whose line group is empty, so a finding whose cited lines were rewritten is no longer recognized as superseded.

Concrete input: citation `"in ddflow/api/review.py:964"`, with `changed` containing `ddflow/api/review.py -> [(960, 980)]` (the HEAD commit rewrote old line 964). Old `_LOC.search` skips `"in"` (no `.` + word char) and returns `group(1)="ddflow/api/review.py"`, `group(2)="964"` → `is_superseded` True → finding is dropped. New `_LOC.search` matches at index 0: `group(1)="in"`, `group(2)=None` → `is_superseded` returns False, so the already-fixed finding is carried forward and re-reported exactly as in bug Be1818cd552. Same for any citation that puts a symbol/word before the location, e.g. ``` `footer()` ddflow/api/review.py:12 ``` (matches `"footer"`), or `"see Makefile:10"` (matches `"see"`). The added test only feeds a bare `"Makefile:10"`/`"p.py:2"`, so it never exercises a citation with a leading token and passes despite the regression.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_is_fix_round` classifies a round as a free "pure fix round" only when every finding of the last round is either in `a["supers"]` (its cited lines were rewritten) or has triage verdict **`"confirmed"`**. It ignores findings whose triage verdict is `"refuted"`, even though the rest of this module treats `refuted` and `confirmed` as equivalent "settled, no further action" states (`_SETTLED = ("refuted", "confirmed")`, and the very next function excludes both from the pending count at line ~496). A refuted finding needs no fix and its lines normally are not rewritten, so it is neither in `a["supers"]` nor `== "confirmed"`.

Concrete failure: round 1 yields f1 and f2; triage refutes f1 and confirms f2; the author commits a fix for f2, rewriting its lines. On re-review with `[review].fix_round_free`, `_superseded` returns `new = {f2}` so `a["supers_new"]` is non-empty and the loop over `found` reaches f1: `f1 not in a["supers"]` and its verdict is `"refuted"`, not `"confirmed"` → `all(...)` is False → `_is_fix_round` returns False. The round is therefore treated as an ordinary delta round that consumes the round budget (the `and not a["fix"]` guard is bypassed from the wrong side), which is exactly the extra re-review/triage cost the change is supposed to remove, for the very common case where round 1 contained any finding the triager rejected. The docstring's own rule ("commits since the reviewed head addressed EVERY finding") already holds here, since a refuted finding is addressed; the code should accept `verdict in _SETTLED` (or `not in ("", None)`) rather than `== "confirmed"`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new branch does not drop a stale finding — it keeps the finding’s full header/detail text in the prompt and then appends an absolute instruction: “do NOT report this finding again”. Combined with the definition given in the message itself (“the lines it cites were rewritten since the reviewed commit”), the suppression condition is broader than the failure the change is supposed to catch (the intent says drop only findings “whose cited lines no longer exist”). Concretely: suppose round‑1 reported finding B against `footer()` citing lines 1740–1744, and the later “fix” commit for an *unrelated* finding A edits one of those same lines (adds a parameter, inserts a guard, reformats the block — very common when A and B live in the same function). `supers` then contains B’s digest, so this loop emits only the SUPERSEDED note instead of B’s triage and tells the reviewer never to re-report it, even though B’s defect (e.g. `footer()` still not consulting `freeexec`) is untouched by A’s commit. The result is a silent false negative — a still-broken HEAD is passed by the gate — which is a worse outcome than the 12 hand-triage calls the bug report was about. The correct predicate is “the cited lines no longer exist / the defect can no longer be located”, not “some line in the cited span changed”; if the decision is to annotate rather than drop, the annotation must not be an unconditional “never report this”, since the code that generated it cannot distinguish an edit that fixed the finding from one that merely landed on the same lines.

chunk_findings.detail: This is prior finding #2, which the author's own triage marks `confirmed`; the probe offered for it ("prompt reworded: do not report this finding again, report only a NEW defect") does not answer it, because the change is wording only — the branch still settles the finding purely on membership in `supers` and still emits an unconditional "do NOT report this finding again". `supers` contains the digest of any prior finding some line of which was touched since the reviewed head, and a fix commit routinely touches a cited line without resolving the cited defect (it can reorder the line, add a guard or comment for a *different* finding, rename a local, or reformat a multi-line expression). Concrete input: a round‑1 finding cites `shell.py:88`; the round‑2 fix commit for an unrelated finding inserts a blank/comment line above `:88` or re-wraps the expression on `:88`, so `changed_old_lines` marks old line 88 changed and the finding's digest lands in `supers`; the round‑2 prompt then prints `SUPERSEDED: the lines it cites were rewritten ... do NOT report this finding again`, so the still-live defect on `shell.py:88` is neither re-reported nor judged against the current code — exactly the false-negative the bug's Expected line ("a re-review judges prior findings against the current code of the files it names") was meant to remove. Prior finding #5's probe ("a live defect on a rewritten line surfaces as a new finding") does not answer this either: the prompt explicitly forbids reporting *this* finding, and the reviewer, seeing the same defect on the same cited line, has no basis to reclassify it as a "NEW defect" rather than the suppressed one, so the wording narrows but does not remove the suppression keyed on line-rewriting instead of defect-resolution.

chunk_findings.detail: `(extra or [])` supplies a **list** as the dict-unpacking operand. Dict unpacking (`{**x}`) requires a mapping, so `{**[]}` raises `TypeError: 'list' object is not a mapping`. The first branch correctly uses `{**(extra or {}), ...}`; this branch does not. The function's own docstring says it adds "what a fix round **/ superseded findings** add", i.e. `supers` is meant to be handled independently of `fix`. So the reachable input is: caller passes `extra=None` (or `{}`, which is falsy) with a non-empty `supers` and `fix=False` — e.g. a re-review round in which the fix commit rewrote some prior findings' cited lines but not all of them. `fix` is `False`, so `extra` is not rewritten in the first branch, `supers` is truthy, and `round_evidence` raises `TypeError` instead of returning the evidence dict with `"superseded"`. Only the accident that `fix=True` rewrites `extra` into a non-empty dict before this line hides the bug in fix rounds.

chunk_findings.detail: The generator takes the **first** path entry that is either an exact match or a basename-suffix match, and discards any later entry — including the exact match. `changed` is built in diff-file order, so when a diff touches two files with the same basename and the *other* one appears first, the exact path is never examined. Concrete input: a finding located at `ddflow/api/__init__.py:12`; the fix commit changed `ddflow/__init__.py` (git orders `ddflow/__init__.py` before `ddflow/api/__init__.py`) and also changed `ddflow/api/__init__.py` line 12. `next` stops on `ddflow/__init__.py` because `"ddflow/__init__.py".endswith("/__init__.py")` is true, gets `ranges` that do not contain 12, and returns `False` — even though the exact entry `ddflow/api/__init__.py` has `(12, 12)`. The finding is therefore *not* marked superseded and is re-raised, which is precisely the Be1818cd552 symptom (a prior finding whose cited line was rewritten is carried forward). The exact match should be preferred over the suffix match before falling back.

chunk_findings.detail: The prior finding #2 ("a fix commit can touch the cited line — reorder it, add a comment, rename a local, reformat — while the original defect still holds, yet the finding is marked SUPERSEDED and the reviewer is told 'do NOT report this finding again'") is still live in this change. The author's probe only says "prompt reworded"; rewording the appended text from "do NOT report it again — judge the new code only" to "do NOT report this finding again; report only a NEW defect of the new code" does not change the decision logic, which is still `f.get("digest") in supers` i.e. "a cited line was rewritten since the reviewed head". Concrete input: round‑1 produces a finding citing `x.py:1`; the next commit edits that line cosmetically (e.g. `x = 1  # FINDME` → `x = 1  # FINDME  # see #12`) without fixing the reported defect. On re‑review `changed_old_lines` contains `x.py:1`, `is_superseded` returns true, the prompt carries only the `SUPERSEDED: … do NOT report this finding again` text, and the still-broken defect is neither re-raised with `triage: untriaged` nor judged. The new test asserts precisely this suppressed behaviour (`assert "SUPERSEDED" in text`, `assert "triage: untriaged" not in text`), so it locks in the gap rather than covering it; the bug's stated expectation is that a re-review "judges prior findings against the current code of the files it names, or drops findings whose cited lines no longer exist", and this case (line still exists, defect still present) is exactly the one left uncured. The probe for #5 ("the operator's spec is exactly that rewritten lines are superseded") is an assertion about a spec that is not in the records given, and it does not answer the substantive point that a persisting defect is suppressed, not re-checked.
